claims.text: A predictive approach integrating machine-learning analysis of atomic-scale vibrational properties and compositional disorder will identify low-phonon-thermal-conductivity high-entropy alloys more accurately than conventional empirical models.
Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is a refractory high-entropy alloy that can be produced through additive manufacturing.
The relevant HfNbTaTiZr material is produced with controlled oxygen and carbon levels.
The processed HfNbTaTiZr maintains either a multiphase microstructure or a metastable single beta-BCC microstructure.
The proposed model incorporates descriptors of atomic vibrational behavior, compositional disorder, and microstructure.
Controlled cooling can determine the phase distribution used as a model descriptor.
Approximately 300–1000 °C is a thermal-insulation-relevant test range for these alloys.
The alloys should be processed under conditions similar to sintering and quenching protocols to obtain the desired microstructures.
A metastable single beta-BCC phase or a controlled multiphase microstructure enhances phonon scattering at grain boundaries and defects.
Enhanced atomic-scale disorder increases phonon scattering.
Multiphase microstructures increase phonon scattering.
The increased phonon scattering lowers phonon thermal conductivity relative to predictions based only on averaged properties.
The proposed approach will identify compositions whose phonon thermal conductivity is approximately 20–30% lower than conventional-model predictions.
The identified compositions will provide improved thermal-insulation performance.
Current prediction methods rely on simple averaging of atomic masses and empirical phase diagrams without detailed vibrational or disorder modeling.
The approach is applicable primarily to refractory high-entropy alloys processed under conditions similar to those studied.
The approach's accuracy may diminish when significant secondary phases form or impurity levels fall outside the studied range.
Processing conditions, impurity levels, and the extent of microstructural disorder affect the magnitude of the phonon-thermal-conductivity reduction.
Laser-flash analysis can provide the phonon thermal conductivity used in the proposed benchmark.
Failure to consistently obtain at least a 20% conductivity advantage over the conventional-model control, or failure to observe the predicted microstructure, is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.
